E1076.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood identifies the philosophers' Metals with the ethereal metals, the Ether's progressive stages from lower to higher forms.
E1076.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood states: “The Metals of the philosophers are the ethereal metals; the Ether’s progressive stages” [APP ¶180]. So the Metals = ethereal metals = the Ether's progressive stages, apparently its processes from lower to higher forms.

E1077.summary: Atwood's term for the condition, proved by ancient experience, of passing beyond ordinary consciousness toward deification.
E1077.body: Atwood speaks of “Such is the condition and metaphysical alienation which ancient experience sublimely proved, as passing to deification” [II.4 ¶49]. The context suggests a passing beyond this life's consciousness; the text links it directly to deification.

E1078.summary: Something to be found and made profitable by joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other.
E1078.body: Atwood describes the procedure of joining it with a consanguineous spirit and circulating the two until one conceives by the other: “this is the true way and means by which the metaphysical body of gold will be made profitable” [III.1 ¶50].

E1079.summary: That which undergoes abyssal regeneration and contest in the intermediate stages before birth into sense perception, and on which the geometric procedure operates.
E1079.body: Atwood speaks of “the abyssal regeneration and contest of the metaphysical Embryo before it is born into the perception by the eye of sense” [III.1 ¶56], placing it in the intermediate stages of the work, before anything becomes visible. Elsewhere she refers to “the geometric method of procedure with the Metaphysical Embryo, through its complex parts” [III.3 ¶37], i.e. the circle–square–triangle–circle procedure; the term is not further defined there.

E1080.summary: A small, purified, fire-tested portion that re-enters its native life and transmutes the whole into its own Aurific Light.
E1080.body: Atwood: “a small grain of the metaphysical ferment leavens the whole lump” [III.1 ¶24]. In the same paragraph she calls it a graft: “the metaphysical graft, already purified and passed the fire, re-enters to redeem its congenital life” [III.1 ¶24], transmuting it all into its own Aurific Light. Leaven and graft are images used for it here, not separate terms.

E1081.summary: The one born in the third vessel, triply covered, represented by the birth of Horus.
E1081.body: Atwood, discussing the birth of Horus, writes: “even so is the metaphysical offspring said to be involved” [IV.2 ¶11], i.e. triply covered and born in the third vessel. Compare the 'supernatural offspring' that Intellect begets [IV.2 ¶7].

E1082.summary: Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood criticizes for reducing the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence.
E1082.body: Atwood rejects their attempt to reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence, saying human instinct opposes it [IV.4 ¶15].

E1083.summary: The analysis of the Universal Subject: separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord, displayed in Valentine's allegory.
E1083.body: Atwood says that in Valentine's allegory “the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis of the Universal Subject is displayed --- the separation, introspection and reunion of the vital elements in their ethereal accord” [III.2 ¶20]; she also inserts “[viz., in the metaphysico-chemical analysis]” into a quoted passage [III.2 ¶19]. These three phases apparently outline the method as she reads it here.

E1084.summary: Atwood's name for the Hermetic science, whose 'Fermentation' she matches with the Kabalah's union with God.
E1084.body: Atwood equates the Kabalah's union with God with “that in metaphysico-chemistry is called Fermentation” [IV.3 ¶27].

E1085.summary: In the Ancient Schools of Divinity, the human Identity's passage out of animal terrene existence through ethereal elements toward the Reason re-entering its First Cause.
E1085.body: Atwood distinguishes the common acceptance of metempsychosis, which she says has bred many errors, from its sense in the Ancient Schools of Divinity: “a transmigrating of the human Identity out of this animal terrene existence through the ethereal elements of its original fundamentals of nature” [IV.2 ¶18], toward the Reason that re-enters its First Cause.

E1086.summary: A quoted speaker whose cosmogony (Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit stirring the mass) Atwood uses as illustration, footnoted to Blackwell's Mythology.
E1086.body: Atwood quotes him: “And know, consecrated Youth, adds the metropolitan of Memphis” [III.3 ¶46]. His account — Chaos, Hyle, Eros, the spirit's breath stirring the mass, and the separation of congenial from heterogeneous parts — illustrates her reading of the work [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶48]; the source is footnoted to Blackwell's Mythology.

E1087.summary: Hermetic writer whom Atwood ranks first among those explaining ancient fable by the Hermetic key, and cites repeatedly for emblems and supporting passages.
E1087.body: Atwood ranks Maier first among those who explained ancient fable by the Hermetic key, though he was profoundly guarded [I.1 ¶70, I.1 n89; works named: Symbola Aurea Mensae, Ulysees, Septimana Philosophica]. He detailed the whole allusion of the epitaph [I.1 ¶24; n31 gives Symbola Auriae Mensa]. She lists him among writers giving specimens of the preliminary lessons, citing Atalanta Fugiens, Emblem 18, for the gold/Mercury passage [III.1 ¶13, III.1 n18]. His Emblema 21 supplies the geometric symbol of the procedure (circle, square, triangle, circle) yielding the Stone: “Fac ex mare et foemina circulum; inde quadrangulum” [III.3 ¶31, III.3 n21]; Atwood calls it 'epigrammatically symbolized by Michael Maier' [III.3 ¶37, III.3 ¶38, III.3 n25]. She places him, with Plato, Proclus, Porphyry, Faber and Tollius, in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil [III.1 ¶25]. His Emblems support the affinity of body and spirit and the agriculture analogy: “Naturam natura docet, debellat ut ignem” [I.3 n37, I.3 n40]. His Hierog. Egypt. Graec. supports the stripping of the Orient Animal: “Animal de Oriente pelle sua leonine spoliari debet” [III.1 ¶64, III.1 n72], given in Latin untranslated (ours: 'the Animal of the East must be stripped of its lion's skin'). Atwood uses him throughout with endorsement.

E1088.summary: Man as the lesser world, comprehending and representing the whole of the macrocosm; the small world in which the work's mysteries are consummated.
E1088.body:
Several voices agree that man is the microcosm. Sendivogius calls it “the lesser world or microcosm” and says “Thou hast in thy body the anatomy of the whole world” [II.1 ¶10]; he also says “man, after the creation of all things, was created into a particular world or microcosm” [II.4 ¶39], on account of the fiery rational soul infused into him. Atwood reports the cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience: “man is a perfect microcosm, wherein, as it was said, the great world and all its creatures might be summarily discerned” [II.1 ¶31]; “man, say they, is demonstrated to be a compendium of the whole created nature” [II.1 ¶32] — while noting this cannot now be proved. In the same context Atwood uses “celeberrimus ille microcosmos et Adam” [II.4 ¶39] (ours: 'that most celebrated microcosm and Adam') alongside the hidden Reason; the referent is unclear.

In her own voice the Microcosm is set against the Great World: it is the scene of “the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation” [III.3 ¶33], and the Archetypal Law is “Perfect in the Microcosmic Unit as in the total Deity of the Great World” [III.3 ¶39]. In the Appendix (later layer): “man, being a microcosm, comprehends and represents the whole and each” of the three Lives, its limbs a laboratory for the spirit [APP ¶35]; and “The whole image of the macrocosm is formed, and has consequently its typical representation, in the Microcosm” [APP ¶55].

E1089.summary: The pairing of individual and universal: the microcosmic experiment yields knowledge of the macrocosmic Cause, and the microcosm's fire continues where the macrocosm's ends.
E1089.body: Atwood: “by the microcosmic experiment into It, the knowledge if the macrocosmic Cause also was derived” [III.1 ¶23] — knowledge of the universal is gained through experiment on the individual. She also speaks of “the corporeal fire of the microcosm” [III.1 ¶37], which takes over where the macrocosm's operative fire ends.

E1090.summary: Three centers in man: head (animal rational life), heart (celestial medial vegetable life), and lumbar region (inferior mineral life).
E1090.body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “There are three microcosmic centers in man” [APP ¶95] — the head, the eye of the Divine and seat of the animal rational life; the heart, of the celestial medial vegetable life; and the lumbar region, of the inferior mineral life. Compare mineral life.

E1091.summary: The inner heaven according to whose magnetic virtue the Spirit displays its properties, and where the rainbow-token of reconciliation appears.
E1091.body: Atwood says the Spirit displays its universal properties internally “according to the magnetic virtue, action, and passion of the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.2 ¶16]; this is not further explained. By analogy with the sky after storm, “the same beautiful token of reconciliation is made apparent in the Microcosmic Heaven” [III.3 ¶13], i.e. the rainbow appears there.

E1092.summary: The life in the individual, which in its natural state resembles the world's vitality taken into the blood by respiration, and needs melioration.
E1092.body: Atwood: “the microcosmic life is not dissimilar from the vitality of the greater world” [II.2 ¶18], which respiration takes into the blood; in its natural state it needs melioration.

E1093.summary: The inner re-creation of man, whose basis is the will as fire.
E1093.body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood says of the will as fire: “it is the basis of our microcosmic recreation” [APP ¶97].

E1094.summary: The tradition Atwood suggests arose from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.
E1094.body: Atwood proposes to show “how the microcosmical tradition arose” [III.3 ¶77]: from the human hypostasis becoming universal intelligence through self-perceivance and voluntary resignation.

E1095.summary: Cited as a contrast: one who preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god.
E1095.body: Atwood uses Midas as a negative example: he preferred an earth-born harmony to the music of the spheres and was dishonored by the god [IV.3 ¶48].

E1096.summary: Cited in support: their 'refined enthusiasm' agrees with the same divine tradition.
E1096.body: Atwood says the 'refined enthusiasm' of the Middle Age Adeptists agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

E1097.summary: The specificative form by which a thing is generated as its own kind; the principle in which Nature contains and separates natures.
E1097.body: In the grain analogy Atwood identifies it: “in its middle principle, that is to say, in the specificative form” [I.3 n40] — the form by which a thing is generated as its own kind. Nature is addressed as that “which containest and separatest natures in a middle principle” [I.3 ¶33]; the Master, quoted, has “which containest and separatest all things in a middle principle” [III.1 ¶49]. So = specificative form.

E1098.summary: Poet quoted from Paradise Lost to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.
E1098.body: Atwood quotes Milton (paradise Lost, 1:676): “That riches grow in hell” [II.3 ¶35, II.3 n41], to illustrate that human works are outdone by spirits reprobate.

E1099.summary: The divine in man, identified with God and Poemander; for Atwood the true Separator, the efficient and regimen of the work, and the Key of the Hermetic Enigma.
E1099.body:
Quoted Hermetic voice: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; Atwood seeks entrance to “the shut palaces of Mind” [II.1 ¶53]. In Hermes' account Poemander says “I am, quoth he, Poemander, the Mind of the Great Lord” [III.3 ¶52] and “I am that Light, the Mind, they God” [III.3 ¶54]; and “That which, in thee, seeth and heareth the Word of the Lord, and the Mind, the Father, God, differ not one from another” [III.3 ¶54]. Mind is always present, comes into the holy and pure, and is “the Porter and Door-keeper” against evil works [III.3 ¶57]. So, per Poemander, Mind = Poemander = Light = God the Father = Porter and Door-keeper. The Rabbi in the Zohar says the articulate voice proceeding from Spirit “comes from the Mind” [III.3 ¶78].

In her own voice, Atwood: “we observe Mind to be the true Separator, the efficient as well as the regimen of the work” [III.1 ¶21]; nothing foreign enters it. And: “Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48]; “no sooner does it attain to Self Knowledge, by proper inquiry within” than the Efficient acts outward [IV.1 ¶48].

E1100.summary: That from which the quintessence is drawn by the magistery; not glossed.
E1100.body: Quoted from Synesius / the New Light: the quintessence is “drawn from its minera by our magistery” [I.2 ¶33]. The term is not glossed; the context shows only that it is that from which the quintessence is drawn.

E1101.summary: The third and lowest life in man, which the Hermetic Art perfects; it contacts the macrocosmic mineral life and first appears in introspection as a dark vapour.
E1101.body: In the Appendix (later layer), Atwood: “The third life, the mineral or lowest life in man” [APP ¶59]; “The Vegetable and Animal lives are higher than the mineral life in us.” [APP ¶59]. The Art is “a perfectioning of the third or lowest or the mineral life in man” [APP ¶44]. It brings one into contact with the Macrocosmic mineral life and is first seen by introspection as a dark vapour. Identity: “The mineral soul or the lowest form of life in us” [APP ¶71] — so = mineral soul. Compare microcosmic centers (lumbar region).

E1102.summary: What is carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury: the root and true matter of the Hermetic Art.
E1102.body: Atwood: “the mineral radix and true mater of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶19], carried in both hands from the Cave of Mercury. So = the true matter of the Art.

E1103.summary: The inner 'secret chamber' guarded by horrors and phantoms.
E1103.body: Atwood speaks of horrors and phantoms “guarding the secret chamber of their mineral soul” [II.3 ¶29]. In the Appendix the mineral soul is identified with the lowest form of life in us (see mineral life).

E1104.summary: The Spirit that acts without intervention or concealment throughout the work.
E1104.body: Atwood: “without intervention or concealment in the ministering Spirit throughout” [III.4 ¶9]. The 'highly effective agent' springing from ourselves, mentioned directly after, apparently refers to it (inferred). Whether 'the Spirit' that some were “compelling the Spirit to their private ends” [III.4 ¶6] is the same is not stated.

E1105.summary: In Norton, the assistants who carry on the work, with stated moral and practical qualifications, numbers and conduct.
E1105.body: Quoted from Norton: “When ye can finde apt Ministers” [III.4 ¶37]; “Noe Minister is apt to this intent But he is sober, wise, and diligent” [III.4 ¶37]. Norton sets out their qualifications, numbers and conduct.
